title: Proof pages for a small clinic
metaTitle: Small clinic case study pages that stay careful
excerpt: A clinic proof page should show the constraint, the decision, and the room with the clinician. End on how a similar patient can book, without promising an outcome you cannot stand behind.
alt: A glass-walled office corridor with a sofa, a floor lamp, and black pendant lights, a real interior a visitor could recognize, for a proof page that should show the actual room.
caption: A glass corridor, a sofa, a lamp. Proof should be a place someone could walk into. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Can a clinic publish a patient story?
faqs.answer: Only with permission, and only with the clinical claim kept inside what you are allowed to say. Show the constraint, the decision about how the visit worked, and the room and clinician. Do not promise that a reader will get the same result. A process story is safer and often more useful than an outcome story.

faqs.question: What if the patient cannot be named?
faqs.answer: You can still describe a situation if it stays true and does not identify them. Skip distinctive details that a neighbor could recognize. If the story only works with those details, do not publish it. An unnamed process page about how a first visit runs can be proof without using a patient at all.

faqs.question: How should the page end?
faqs.answer: Tell a similar patient how to book, what the visit is called, and what to have ready. Do not end on a transformation. The last lines should be the path: the booking, the phone, and the boundary if this story is not their situation.

markdown:
A small clinic case study page should show the constraint, the decision, and the room with the clinician. A patient who is already anxious is reading to see how a visit like theirs is handled. Screenshots of a smiling face, with no decision, are decoration.

End on a booking. Tell a similar patient how to book a visit. Do not end on a cure. A proof page that promises a result you cannot repeat is a clinical claim hiding in a marketing layout.

## Start from the constraint, not the recovery

The constraint is why the story is worth telling. A patient who had never been to a clinic and needed to know the fee before they traveled. A referrer who needed a written plan the same day. A room that is up a flight of stairs, and a visit designed so people know that before they arrive. Write the limit first.

Google's notes on how content earns trust point to evidence of the work: what was done, and photographs, not a claim with nothing beside it. A clinic story can follow that shape without becoming a case report. The work is the visit design. The photograph is the room and the clinician. The claim stops where your professional rules stop.

Be plain about what kind of patient this was, without identifying them. Age band only if it matters and does not single them out. The kind of visit. The worry they arrived with, if they agreed you could share it. "A new patient who was afraid the first visit would include a procedure" is a constraint. "Jane, 42, from the flat above the bakery, whose scan showed..." is an identification risk and a clinical overshare. Choose the first.

Do not open with the happiest possible ending. Readers who are anxious will feel managed. They want to know what happened in the awkward middle: the arrival, the explanation, the moment they could have left.

## The decision the clinic made

The middle of the page is a decision about care delivery, not a miracle. What you changed in the visit so the constraint was handled. What you refused to do.

Decisions that make honest proof:

- You show the fee and the stairs on the page, because surprise at the door was the complaint.
- You split examination and procedure into different visits, so a first appointment stays a conversation.
- You name the clinician at booking, because not knowing who would be in the room was stopping people from coming.
- You decline a visit you cannot support and say so in the story, including where you sent the patient.

Write the refusal at the same size as the success. A proof page of uninterrupted wins reads as an advert, and anxious patients are already scanning for the advert. The boundary is the reassuring part. It should match the boundary on the services page. If the story shows you doing something the services page says you never do, fix one of them before either stays online.

Name the staff role that made the call. "The front desk started telling people about the stairs when they booked" is a decision. "We strive for excellence" is not. Proof is operational. A small clinic has the advantage that the operation is visible. Use that.

## The room and the clinician in the frame

Show the room the story talks about. The chairs, the light, the step. If the story is about a conversation before any procedure, do not illustrate it with a dramatic instrument. The picture should match the decision. A caption can carry the fact. "The first-visit room. Procedures happen in a different visit, if they happen at all."

Put the clinician in the same story, doing the job you named. A portrait in the corridor is enough if the corridor is real and the caption says they lead this visit. A stock smile is not a stand-in. If you do not have permission to show a patient, do not imply a model is the patient. Say "the clinician in the first-visit room" and stop.

Alt text describes what is in the frame. "Clinician standing beside the treatment chair in a small room with a window" is alt text. "Best clinic for pain" is a slogan stuffed into an image, and it fails anyone who cannot see the photo. The adjacent paragraph holds the meaning. The picture cannot be the only place the fact exists. Write the fact in the sentence.

One or two frames. A gallery of the renovation is a different page. Patients are not hiring your architect. They are deciding whether they can walk into this room with this person.

## What you may say about the result

Say what changed in the process. They knew the fee before they traveled. They met the named clinician. They left with a written plan or a referral. Those are results you can stand behind if they are true and typical.

Do not invent a clinical statistic. Do not borrow a percentage from a paper you did not run. Do not write "90 percent of patients" because it sounds like proof. If you have a real count from your own diary, and you are allowed to share it, define the period and the denominator in the same sentence. If you do not, leave the number out. A clinic page with a fake cure rate is worse than a short page.

Quotes need a name or a clear statement that the patient asked not to be named, plus permission, plus a fact. "They made the stairs clear before I booked" is a quote about the decision. "They changed my life" is a quote you should decline unless you are prepared for it to be read as a promise. You are usually not.

Mark the limit. "This is how a first visit goes for this kind of problem. It is not a promise about the medical result." That sentence keeps the page useful and keeps it in its lane. Google's trust emphasis on health topics is a reason to be dull on purpose. Dull and accurate is a kindness.

## A structure someone can read while worried

Keep the page short enough to finish. Open with the constraint in two sentences. Then the decision. Then the room and the person. Then what the patient can expect, and what they should not expect. Then who this is not for. Then the booking.

A shape that holds:

1. The situation, without a name if a name is risky.
2. What the clinic decided to do differently.
3. The room and the clinician.
4. What a similar patient can count on.
5. Who should not use this story as a map.
6. How to book the visit the story describes.

"Who should not" matters. If the story depended on an in-person visit, say that video is a different path. If it depended on no referral, do not let a patient who needs one think they can skip it. Edges make the middle more believable.

Use the same visit name as the services page and the diary. A proof page that invents a new name for the appointment creates a third product. The patient will not know which button to press.

## End on the booking

The last section is practical. If this sounds like your situation, book this visit. Say what to have ready. A referral if required. The fee, repeated. The question they can ask the desk. Give them the phone as well as the button. A person who has just read about someone else's fear may prefer a voice.

Do not attach a second, more expensive procedure as the "next step" at the bottom. That turn makes the story feel like a funnel. If a later visit sometimes follows, mention it as a possibility the clinician will discuss, not as a button. The only button should be the visit the story was about.

If you cannot offer that visit this month, do not publish a booking button that fails. Say the diary is closed and how the waitlist works, or unpublish the page until the path is real. A proof page with a broken ending confirms the anxiety it was meant to ease.

[Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) shows how a public project is framed around a constraint and a decision. A clinic proof page wants that editing, with a stricter rule on claims. The photograph is the room. The result is the process you can keep.

## Permission, storage, and when to take it down

Written permission should say what you may show and for how long. Store it with the page, not in a personal inbox. On a Hanabi project the portal holds docs and assets so the next person can see what was agreed. The public page stays small. The permission stays findable.

Review the page when the room changes, the clinician leaves, or the visit is redesigned. A story about a person who no longer works there, illustrated with a room you remodeled, is fiction. Fiction is not proof. Take it down or rewrite it with current facts.

Give one person the job of unpublishing. Committees are how stale clinical stories survive. A small clinic can move faster than a hospital intranet. Use that speed on the way down, not only on the way up.

Readers who believe the story still have to find it, and find the booking, without wandering a departmental menu. [Navigation for a small clinic](/blog/navigation-for-a-small-clinic) is about labeling the jobs patients already have words for, including the path into a page like this.
